A free estimate comes first.

sections.heading: Why a Warm Plate Is Worth a Call
body: Outlets wear out. Plugs get pulled in and out for years, and the metal inside stops gripping. Most of what goes wrong is one of a short list of things.

items.title: The plate is warm or discolored
items.text: A loose connection makes heat, and heat is how outlets fail badly. Stop using it and call.

items.title: It buzzes, crackles or smells like burning
items.text: That's arcing, and it needs attention now. Unplug what you can, switch off the breaker if you know which one it is, and call.

items.title: It's dead
items.text: Often a tripped breaker or a tripped GFCI somewhere else. If the reset doesn't bring it back, a wire behind the outlet has likely come loose.

items.title: It only takes two prongs
items.text: An older outlet with no ground hole can't properly protect a modern plug. Grounding circuits is part of what we do.

sections.quote: If you need any electrical work done you have to call them. Very professional and clean work in a timely manner, with very fair prices.

sections.heading: Replacing a Worn Outlet
body: Most bad outlets are fixed by replacing the outlet itself, not by rewiring the room. A new one grips plugs again and carries its load without heating up.
If the trouble is in the wiring behind it, the repair is bigger.
Switches, dimmers and fixtures wear the same way, and we repair them too.

sections.heading: Kitchen and Bath Outlets That Keep Tripping
body: Outlets in kitchens, bathrooms, garages and outdoors are usually GFCI protected. A GFCI cuts the power fast when current goes where it shouldn't.
One that trips over and over, or won't reset, is either doing its job or has failed. Either way it's worth a look.

sections.heading: Why an Old Bedroom Outlet Runs Warm
body: Older houses were wired when a room needed a lamp and a radio. Now it's a TV, a game console, chargers and a space heater, all on circuits sized for less.
A warm outlet in an older room is often carrying more than the circuit was built for.

sections.heading: Before You Call, Look at the Breaker Panel
body: If you can do it safely, unplug what's on the outlet and look for a tripped breaker. Check the GFCI buttons on outlets in the kitchen, bath, garage or outside, and press reset.
If the outlet is scorched or smells like burning, stop using it.

sections.heading: A Charger You Already Bought, a Car You Haven't

image.alt: Electrical panel with breakers and labeled circuits

body: Tell us the charger you have or want, the car, and where it parks.
A free estimate comes first.

sections.heading: What a Charger Install Needs
body: A plug-in charger on a regular outlet adds range slowly. Most people who own an electric car want a faster one, and a faster one asks more of your house.

items.title: A circuit of its own
items.text: A faster home charger usually runs on a dedicated 240-volt circuit. It shouldn't share a breaker with anything else.

items.title: A panel with room
items.text: Your panel has to have space and capacity for the new circuit. In an older house, or one already running AC and other big loads, that's the first thing to check.

items.title: A run from the panel to the garage
items.text: The wire has to get from the panel to the charger. The shorter and more direct the route, the simpler the job.

items.title: A good spot on the wall
items.text: The cable has to reach the car's charging port, and the charger has to be where you can use it and where it's protected from the weather.

items.title: The right size for the car
items.text: Your car can only accept so much power. A bigger charger doesn't charge it faster than the car allows.

sections.heading: On the Garage Wall or the Outside Wall?

sections.heading: Look Up Two Things Before You Buy
